# Keeping and exchanging a song {#sec-files}

A native song and a MIDI file serve different purposes. The native file keeps
Modal's working structure and settings. A Standard MIDI File exchanges events
with other software. Choosing the right one avoids mistaking a useful
interchange copy for a complete working document.

## Native files keep the arrangement

The `.modal` format stores sections, track settings, local meters and the
musical events in plain text. A track's drum-map names are embedded too,
so moving the song preserves them without a separate map file. Positions within the file belong to sections,
so moving a section need not rewrite every event's position in the document.
The file can be inspected or kept in version control, but editing it by hand
is not required for normal work.

`:w` saves the current native song. A new song opens Modal's file picker; `:w FILE`
saves to a named file. With no extension Modal adds `.modal`. `:wq` saves
and quits. Native saves use a temporary file and replacement to avoid leaving
a partially written song if writing fails.

To keep the version on disk and carry on in a copy, save as another file with
`:song-save-as`. It opens the picker in the song's folder with its current
name suggested, so changing a word or adding a number is quick. From then on
the song belongs to the new file, and `:w` saves there; the old file stays as
it was last saved.

## Backups: the versions a save replaces

Saving is quick, so it's easy to save over something you wanted to keep: a
take you liked before a transform, or the arrangement before you moved the
chorus. So each time a save replaces a song file, Modal first keeps the file
as it was. The newest of these backups is backup 1; at the next save it
becomes backup 2, and so on, the oldest dropping off after five. Think of them
as the last few saves, newest at the top of the pile.

`, f b` (`:song-backups`, mnemonic **b**ackup) lists the current song's
backups, with when each version was saved, such as `saved today 14:02` or
`saved yesterday 18:30`. Choose one with Up and Down and press Enter: it opens
as a new song alongside the others, without a file, and the song you were in
stays exactly as it was. So you can listen to the old version, copy a phrase or
a track back from it (see Copying between songs below), or switch between the
two with `]f` and `[f` to compare. To go back to it altogether, save it over
the song with `:w! FILE`; saving it plainly asks where, so it never replaces
the song by accident. Escape leaves the list.

The backups are kept in Modal's state directory (the file picker's **State**
place), away from the song's folder so they don't clutter it or its version
control. They belong to the song's file by its full path: a song moved or
renamed starts a new set, and its old backups stay under the old path.
`set backups=10` in `modalrc` keeps more, and `0` keeps none. If a backup
can't be made, as when the disk is full, the song is still saved and the
message says that no backup was made and why.

Nothing is backed up the first time a new song is saved, as there is nothing
yet to replace, and exporting a MIDI file makes no backups.

`:song-open-copy FILE`, which `, f b` uses, opens a copy of any song file in
the same way, as a new song without a file: a convenient way to start a song
from another one used as a template.

## A song's title

A filename has to suit the computer: short, unique in its folder, often with a
date or a version number. A song's title is what you call it, such as
*Morning*, and it travels with the song whatever the file is called. So
`morning-v3.modal` and `morning-v4.modal` can both be *Morning*, told apart by
their files.

`, f t` (`:song-title`, mnemonic **t**itle) sets it. Modal asks for the title
with the current one ready to edit; Enter keeps the answer, an empty answer
clears the title, and Escape leaves it as it was. `:song-title Morning` sets it
directly. Setting the title is one undo step, and the song counts as changed
until it's saved, because the title is saved with it. A new song has no title,
and saving never invents one from the filename.

Where a song has a title, Modal shows it first and the file after it:

- the window's title bar reads `Morning (morning-v3.modal) – Modal`, with
  `[+]` before the dash while there are unsaved edits, `(unsaved)` for a song
  without a file, and `(demo.mid, imported)` for an imported MIDI file;
  without a title it shows the filename alone. The status line shows only
  `+`, so the full name is a key away: `Ctrl-g`, as in Vim, says the title,
  the file (with `~` for your home folder), whether it is modified and the
  song's length, such as `"Morning" · ~/Songs/morning-v3.modal · modified ·
  24 bars, 0:48`;
- the open-songs and recent-songs lists give the title a column of its own
  before the filename;
- the arrangement shows it at the top left of the track headers.

An imported MIDI file takes its title from the name of its first track, when
that track is a conductor track holding the tempo and meter, and `:export`
writes the title back there, as other sequencers expect.

## The Files keys

The everyday file commands have keys in the leader's **Files** group,
`, f`. After `, f`, pause to see the menu:

| Keys | Does | Same as |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `, f f` | Open a song or import a MIDI file, choosing it in the picker (**f**ind a file) | `:e` |
| `, f o` | Switch to another **o**pen song | `:song-select` |
| `, f n` | Start a **n**ew song alongside the others | `:new` |
| `, f s` | **S**ave | `:w` |
| `, f S` | Save as another file (a capital for the bigger save) | `:song-save-as` |
| `, f c` | **C**lose this song | `:song-close` |
| `, f x` | E**x**port a Standard MIDI File | `:export` |
| `, f i` | **I**mport tracks from a song or MIDI file | `:track-import` |
| `, f r` | Open a **r**ecently used song | `:song-recent` |
| `, f t` | Set the song's **t**itle | `:song-title` |
| `, f b` | Open a **b**ackup of this song as a new song | `:song-backups` |

The keys run the plain forms of the commands, so none of them discards unsaved
edits: closing a song with edits is refused until it is saved, or closed with
`:song-close!`.

## Working with several songs

Open another song with `:e FILE` or create one with `:new`. Each open song
keeps its own unsaved edits and undo history. Opening the same file again
selects its existing copy. Opening a file from a sole, untouched new song
uses that song's place in the list.

Use `:song-select` (`, f o`) to see the open songs. The list shows each
song's title, its file name, and the folder it's in, each in a column of its
own. A song without a title leaves that column blank, and when no open song
has a title the column is left out. A new song is named **Untitled 2** or
similar, with **Unsaved** for its folder, and an imported file's folder is
labelled **MIDI import**. The active song starts
highlighted and has a `›` mark. A `+` marks unsaved edits. Type part of a
title, name or folder to narrow the list, use Up and
Down to choose, and press Enter to switch. Escape cancels. Long paths can
wrap under the highlighted row's list. Switching stops playback. Stop
recording and let the take finish before changing songs.

Each song remembers where you were in it. Coming back to a song shows the
view you left it in, with every view's cursor, scroll and zoom as they were:
the piano roll returns to the same page and pitch, with each track's fold
choice, and the arrangement to the same tracks and bars. Backspace, `''` and
`gv` go back through that song's own places, and Space plays from its own
play-from marker (▶). So you can leave the piano roll of one song in the
middle of a phrase, check something in another song, and come back ready to
carry on. A song opened or created for the first time starts at its
beginning, in the view you were using.

Macros, the last search, settings and toggles are shared between songs.
These places last while Modal is running; closing a song or reloading
it with `:e!` starts it afresh.

When two or three songs are open, stepping between them is quicker than
choosing. `]f` goes to the next open song and `[f` to the one before, in the
chooser's order, as `]s` and `[s` step through sections. They go round at
either end, so with three songs open, `]f` from the last returns to the first.
A count steps further: `2]f` skips a song. Ctrl-Tab and Ctrl-Shift-Tab do the
same, as they move between tabs in a web browser. The message row names the
song reached and its place, such as `Song 2 of 3: Morning`, by its
title where it has one and otherwise by its file.

`:song-close` closes the current song and requires `!` if it has unsaved
edits. The last close leaves a new untitled song. `:q` (or `:qa`) quits only
when all open songs have been saved or are unchanged. `:wq` saves the current
song and checks the other open songs before quitting. `:q!` explicitly
discards all remaining unsaved edits.

With several songs changed, save them all at once with `:wa` (**w**rite
**a**ll). Songs that already have files are saved straight away; then Modal
shows each new song in turn while the picker asks where to keep it, so you
always know which song you're naming. The message says how many were saved,
such as `Saved 3 songs`. Cancelling a picker stops there, saying what was
saved so far. `:wqa` (or `:xa`) does the same and then quits, which makes it
the quickest way to end a session safely.

Closing the window asks first if any song has unsaved changes, whichever song
is showing. It names them, by title or else by file, such as
`3 songs have changes not saved: plain.modal, Morning and Untitled 3`. **Save
all** saves them as `:wqa` does and closes; **Don't save** closes without
saving; **Cancel** goes back to work.

`:e! FILE` and `:new!` replace the current song and can discard its unsaved
edits. Use the plain forms to keep it open.

## Going back to recent songs

Modal keeps a list of the song files you have opened or saved lately, so
yesterday's work is a couple of keys away. `, f r` (`:song-recent`) shows it,
newest first, in columns: the song's title, the file's name, the folder it's
in, and when you last used it, such as `today 17:42`, `yesterday 09:10`,
`Mon 18 Nov` or, from an earlier year, `2 Mar 2025`. The title is the one the
song had when you last opened or saved it, so a title just changed shows here
once the song is saved. When no listed song has a title, the title column is
left out.

Type part of a title, name or folder to narrow the list, use Up and Down to choose,
and press Enter to open the song, or to switch to it if it's already open.
Escape leaves the list. Delete takes the highlighted entry off the list; it
never touches the file itself. A file that has been moved or deleted shows
`not found`, and choosing it offers to take it off the list.

Opening a song by any route counts, as does saving one. A MIDI file you
imported is listed until you save it as a song, when the song takes its
place. New songs that haven't been saved yet aren't listed. The list keeps 12
songs; `set recentsongs=20` in `modalrc` keeps more, and `0` keeps none.

## Copying between songs

The registers are shared by every open song, so copying from one song to
another needs no new keys: yank in one, switch with `]f` or `, f o`, and put
in the other. What changes is what the material meets when it arrives: other
tracks, other sections, other bars and another tempo. Modal keeps the music
as it was and fits it in as follows.

**Notes keep their timing.** Material keeps its length in time and plays at
the destination's tempo, since tempo belongs to the whole song and can't
travel with part of it. Every song Modal opens is converted to the same
resolution, so nothing is rounded on the way.

**Whole bars bring their bars.** If you took bars whole, with `yy` or `dd`
(`2yy` for two), `yab`, a section's time with `yas`, a whole track with `yit`,
or bars selected in the arrangement, the bar lines come with them. Copy two
bars of a 7/8 riff from one song into a 4/4 song, and the notes land at the
same times; the track they land on takes the riff's 7/8 as a meter of its own
over those bars, then rejoins the song's 4/4, with a short bar in between if
the riff ends partway through one. The rest of the song stays in 4/4. The
message says so: `…, keeping its 7/8`.

**A bar's events are just notes.** `yib` and `yis` take the events in a bar
or section, not the bars, and other motions and selections take a stretch of
time. These land in the destination's bars, so the same riff copied with
`yib` simply sits in 4/4. Either way you can change your mind afterwards:
`, s f` sets a track following the song's meter again, and `, b m` rebars a
selection.

**Sections find their tracks by name.** A section taken from the section
strip with `Y` brings its own meter, tempo and labels. Its notes go to the
tracks with the same names in the destination: the source's Bass part to the
destination's Bass track, wherever that track is in the list. A source track
with no match is added at the end, with its settings, and the message names
it, so nothing is dropped.

**Whole tracks are laid along time.** A track yanked with `, t y` and put
with `, t p` brings its settings: port, channel, drum map and playback
transforms. In a song with different sections, it is laid along time from the
song's start and cut where the destination's sections begin. If it runs past
the end, a section is added to hold the rest, named in the message. Where
its bars differ from the song's, it keeps them as its own meter. Because a
section always starts a bar, a destination section beginning partway through
one of the track's bars cuts that bar there.

Each put is a single undo step, including any tracks or sections it added.

## Importing tracks from a file

Sometimes you want a part from another file without opening the whole song:
a drum pattern from a MIDI file, or a bass line from an older version of a
song. `, f i` (`:track-import`, or `:read` for short) brings tracks from a
`.modal` or `.mid` file straight into the song you're working on. It always
reads the file as saved on disk, which also makes it a way to recover a track
you have since spoiled.

After choosing the file in the picker, a list shows the file's tracks by
their numbers in that file, with each one's channel, how many notes it has
and its drum map, if any, to help tell the parts apart. Nothing is ticked at
first. Move with Up and Down (or `j` and `k`) and press Space to tick or
untick the highlighted track; `a` ticks every track, or clears the ticks
once every one is ticked. The message row says how many are ticked.

Enter imports the ticked tracks, or the highlighted one if none are ticked,
so bringing in a single part is just moving to it and pressing Enter. Escape
leaves without importing. Enter works by running the `:read` line that names
the same tracks, such as `:read ~/Songs/Groove.modal 1,3-5`, and that line
goes into the command line's history: press `:` and Up to repeat the import
or change which tracks it takes.

The tracks go in after the cursor's track, in their order in the file, with
their settings, exactly as whole tracks copied from another song do: laid
along time, keeping their own bars, and with a section added if they run past
the end of the song. Only tracks come in. Your song keeps its own sections,
labels and tempo; if the file's tempo differs, the message says so, as in
`its tempo was 100, this song plays at 120`. To take more of a file, open it
as a song with `:e` and copy what you need across.

On the command line, name the tracks after the filename to import without
the list: `:read Groove.mid 1,3-5,7` takes tracks 1, 3, 4, 5 and 7, and
`:read Groove.mid all` every track. A number the file doesn't have is
refused with the reason, as in `No track 9: the file has 5`. Like the
other file commands, importing is refused while recording, and the whole
import is one undo step.

The native `.modal` file format is still under development. Compatibility
between files written by different development versions is not yet guaranteed.
Keep separate copies of important work before trying a newer build.
Undo history is a working-session facility, not a substitute for saved copies.

## Choosing a file {#sec-file-picker}

The picker lets you see the directory as you type or browse. `:e` opens it
beside the current song, or for a new song in your Songs folder, which is
your home folder until you choose one (see below). `:w` and
`:wq` use it when the song needs a filename, and `:song-save-as` always does.
`:export` with no filename opens it beside the song too, listing MIDI files
and suggesting the song's name as a `.mid` file. Drum-map commands without a
filename start in the reusable maps directory. `:write-config` starts in
the configuration directory and suggests `modalrc`.

Use Up and Down to choose a row and Enter to open it. A folder leads to its
contents, and `../` goes up to the parent. Alt-Down opens **Places**, where
you can jump to **Songs**, **This song's folder** (when the song has a file),
**Home**, **Config**, **Drum maps** or **State**. For example, **State** is
useful when opening a recovered song. Escape backs out of Places or cancels
the picker.

If you keep your songs in one folder, tell Modal where it is with a line in
`modalrc`, such as `set songfolder=~/Music/Songs` (see @sec-customisation).
A new song then opens and saves there, typed paths such as `:e Ideas/Riff`
start there, and Places lists it first as **Songs**, followed by
`(songfolder)` as a reminder of the setting that moves it. Until you set it,
Songs is your home folder. A song that already has a file always starts
beside its own file instead, so working on a song keeps you near it. Modal
doesn't create the folder: if it's missing, Places marks it
`(songfolder, not found)`.

Typing narrows the list. Tab completes the common part of matching names
and then cycles through the choices. Completed folders end in `/` so you
can keep completing inside them. You can also type an absolute path, or a
path relative to the folder shown.

When saving, Enter on an empty filename accepts the suggestion. Type another
name to save elsewhere. If a file already exists, Modal asks before replacing
it. Press `n` or Escape to return to the picker and choose a different name.

## Importing MIDI

`:e FILE.mid` imports a Standard MIDI File, as does passing it to Modal at
startup. Import produces a Modal song that can then be saved natively.
A subsequent MIDI export is an interchange operation, not an instruction
to replace the native working copy.

A Modal track uses one output channel. MIDI material with multiple channels
is separated as needed on import, so its parts can have independent settings.
The conductor holds tempo and meter, while imported labels can describe
places in the song. `:label-to-section` (`, s l`) can turn those places into an
editable section structure once their meaning is understood.

Imported data is retained honestly, including unusual timing and overlapping
notes. An edit may refuse a new collision even though imported overlaps
already exist: preserving supplied data and creating more of it are separate
responsibilities.

## Exporting MIDI

`:export FILE.mid` writes a Standard MIDI File; with no filename it opens the
file picker (@sec-file-picker). Export uses the stored events and their channels. Playback-only
transpose, velocity, timing and quantise settings are not all baked into it,
and mute or solo does not select a subset for export. Freeze a chosen
playback result first when the destination should receive those changes.

Track bank and program setup is an exception: it is written at the start
so that the receiving program can choose the requested sound. Reimporting
that file reads those setup messages as events, because MIDI does not mark
them as Modal-specific track settings.

The conductor's meter becomes the MIDI file's shared time signature. Independent
track meters, section editing structure, machine routing and Modal's working
state cannot all be represented by that shared interchange model. A `.mid`
export should therefore accompany, rather than replace, the native song
when those distinctions matter.

An existing named output file is protected from accidental overwrite.
The bang follows the command, as in `:export! FILE.mid` or `:w! FILE`.
It does not go at the end of the path. Choosing an existing file in the
picker asks before replacing it.

Each command keeps to its own kind of file, because a file is read back by
its name: `:w` refuses a name ending `.mid` or `.midi`, and `:export` one
ending `.modal`, each saying which command writes that kind.

## File-command summary

| Command | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `:e` / `:e FILE` | Choose or name a song or MIDI file to open |
| `:new` | Open a new untitled song |
| `:song-select` | List and switch between open songs |
| `:song-title [TITLE]` | Set the song's title, asking with it ready to edit without TITLE |
| `:song-close[!]` | Close the current song, with `!` to discard its unsaved edits |
| `:w` / `:w FILE` | Save the native song, or save to a chosen path |
| `:song-save-as[!] [FILE]` | Save as another file, choosing it in the picker without FILE |
| `:track-import [FILE [TRACKS]]` | Import tracks from a song or MIDI file, choosing which (also `:read`) |
| `:export` / `:export FILE.mid` | Write a MIDI interchange copy |
| `:q` / `:qa` | Quit, protecting unsaved changes in every open song |
| `:wq` | Save and quit |
| `:wa` | Save every song with unsaved changes, asking where to keep each new one |
| `:wqa` / `:xa` | Save every song with unsaved changes, then quit |
| `:song-backups` | List the song's backups, to open one as a new song |
| `:song-open-copy FILE` | Open a copy of a song file as a new song without a file |
| `:source` | Re-read application configuration; it does not open a song |
| `:write-config` | Write application preferences; it does not save the song |
| `:drum-map-load [FILE]` | Load a drum map into the current track, or choose a file |
| `:drum-map-save[!] [FILE]` | Save a reusable map; `!` reviews an existing copy before replacing it |

Relative song paths start in the song's folder, or the home folder for an
unsaved song. Configuration commands use the configuration directory instead;
drum-map files start in its `drum-maps/` subdirectory. See @sec-drum-maps for
map ownership and comparison.
Completion shows the base directory when offering filenames. A path beginning
with `~` starts at the home directory.

## When the result is unexpected

The most useful first evidence is the message row. A refused operation leaves
a reason there: an overlap, an unavailable port, an invalid value or a recording
track that cannot be edited yet. Repeating the same keys without considering
the reason will usually repeat the same refusal.

If notes appear in the right place but sound different, inspect track playback
settings and the receiving instrument's program and controllers. If a MIDI
export sounds different in another program, check which playback transforms
still need freezing and how that program chooses its instruments. If input
activity is visible but silent, distinguish input reception, arming, Thru,
output routing and the receiver's audio path.

For a reproducible problem, keep a small song that demonstrates it, the exact
commands or keys, the operating system and the relevant MIDI route. The
state directory's `crash.log`, if present, records unexpected application
errors with a version and time. This is more useful than assuming that every
silence or warning is a timing problem.

If Modal ever does stop on such an error while a song has unsaved changes, it
saves the song as it was into the state directory, named `recovered-` and the
time, and says where when it next starts. Open that file with `:e`, save it
under the name it should have with `:w FILE`, then delete the recovered copy.
It is a last resort rather than a substitute for saving.

If a save replaced something you wanted, `, f b` lists the versions it
replaced; see Backups above.

## Companion command-line tools

`modal-ports` lists visible inputs and outputs. `modal-play` and `modal-record`
provide terminal-based MIDI playback and recording with their own `--help`.
They are separate programs, not commands for Modal's colon prompt.

`modal-loopback` measures timing through a real MIDI route. Its results depend
on the interface, driver and test setup. Software tests and offscreen figures
do not measure those hardware properties. The repository's `docs/tools.md`
contains the detailed diagnostic options; most musical work should begin
with the GUI's port and track information instead.
